chunks: Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya narrated from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from Ibn Fadhl, from Uthman ibn Ghaleb, from Ruh ibn Abd al-Rahim, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him)

From a slave who sought protection from his master, and he consumed a great deal of wealth, he said: 'There is no liability on his master, but it is upon the slave, and they do not sell him, but he is given respite (to pay), and if his master places him under restriction (of property), there is no liability on the master nor on the slave.'

key_terms.حَجَرَ عَلَيْهِ: He placed him under restriction (of property/finances)
key_terms.يُسْتَسْعَى: He is given respite/time to pay

ai.seo_question: What is the financial liability of a master when his slave consumes wealth while acting as a guarantor?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* clarifies the mechanics of *istijrar* (guaranteeing a transaction) within the context of slavery, establishing that the slave bears the financial burden for consumed wealth while the master is exempt from direct liability. It further delineates the master's recourse, prohibiting immediate sale for debt recovery in favor of granting respite (*istis'a*), unless the master had previously restricted the slave's financial autonomy, in which case the liability dynamics shift. This ruling highlights the nuanced balance between the master's ownership rights and the slave's emerging financial agency in Shia jurisprudence.
